tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

content.content:
# Switchboard — build round

Build the first version of **Switchboard**, a shared team inbox. Customers
write to a business over a messaging provider. Support agents (people who work
at that business) log in, see conversations arrive in real time, reply, and
leave private notes for each other.

Several businesses (workspaces) use the same deployment. They must never see
each other's data.

**You will not finish everything below.** That is intended. Build the product
first, then make it survive: a small product that keeps working when the
network is bad, the process dies or a second copy is started beats a large one
that works only on the happy path.

Use any AI tools you like. You own every line you submit: in the follow-up
call we open your code, ask why it is the way it is, and debug it with you.

## The two hours

| Time | What |
| --- | --- |
| 0:00 – 0:10 | Read `START_HERE.md` and this brief. Start the services. |
| 0:10 – 1:50 | Build. Commit at least every 15 minutes. |
| 1:50 – 2:00 | Run the full check, push, make the repository public, send the form. See `SUBMISSION.md`. |

The form closes at 2:00. What counts is the commit you name in the form.

## How it fits together

```
simulated customers -> Pigeon :4010 --webhook POST--> YOUR SERVER --WebSocket--> YOUR REACT APP
        (given)          (given)                      (you build)                 (you build)

agent types a reply -> YOUR SERVER -> POST /v1/messages on Pigeon -> status webhooks back to you
```

You build the business side only. The customers are simulated and live inside
Pigeon; there is no customer app, and they do not answer your replies.

| Service | Port | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pigeon | 4010 | The messaging provider (simulated). Sends you webhooks, accepts your sends. Unreliable on purpose. See `PIGEON.md`. |
| Mock IdP | 4020 | OpenID Connect provider with five test users. Discovery at `/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Client id `switchboard-web`. PKCE (S256) is required. |
| MongoDB | 27017 | Real. |
| Redis | 6379 | Real. |
| Elasticsearch | 9200 | Real, optional: `npm run up:search`. |
| Paybox | 4030 | Simulated payment provider. Only for the bonus. See `PAYBOX.md`. |

`scaffold/` is an optional empty shell (Express + TypeScript server, Vite +
React app, already pointed at the services). It has no product code. Use it,
or delete it and bring your own Node stack; then change the `start` command in
`switchboard.json`.

## What to build

### The product
1. **Login.** Sign in through the IdP (authorization code + PKCE). A user's
   workspaces and roles come from the `workspaces` claim. Roles: `admin`, `agent`.
2. **Receive messages.** Accept Pigeon webhooks at `POST /webhooks/pigeon`.
   Pigeon is not a friendly network: read `PIGEON.md` before you write this.
3. **Inbox.** Conversations per contact, newest activity first, paginated.
   Open a conversation and read its messages in order. An agent can claim a
   conversation; two agents cannot both hold it. Close and reopen.
4. **Reply.** An agent replies and the message goes out through Pigeon. The
   agent sees its status: queued, sent, delivered, failed. A customer must
   never receive the same reply twice, and a reply must not be lost.
5. **Real time.** New messages, status changes and assignments appear without
   a refresh (WebSockets). A client that drops and reconnects misses nothing.
6. **Frontend.** A React app an agent could actually use for the above.

### Making it survive: the five levels
The automatic check has five levels. Each is worth points on its own. You can
run all of them yourself except level 4.

| Level | Situation | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | One copy of your server. Webhooks arrive duplicated, out of order, forged and replayed. Pigeon rate-limits you, answers slowly, and goes down for a while. Six agents claim one conversation in the same instant. | 24 |
| 2 | Your server is **killed without warning** (`kill -9`) and started again a few seconds later: once in the middle of a flood of webhooks, once just after it accepted a batch of replies. Nothing may be lost, duplicated or sent twice. | 14 |
| 3 | **Several copies** of your server run behind a load balancer and share MongoDB and Redis. Everything in level 1 must still hold, the rate limit is per workspace and not per copy, and when one copy dies for good the others finish its work within 60 seconds. | 22 |
| 4 | **The written rules.** Not in the check you can run. We send your server the awkward cases that `PIGEON.md` ("How your endpoint must answer") and the contract below describe in words. Ten rules, one point each. | 10 |
| 5 | **Login, tenant isolation and real time**, with several copies running. The check signs in through the IdP as a browser would, calls your API as a user of one workspace, and listens on your WebSocket while customers write. | 15 |

### Also valued (reviewed, not checked automatically)
- **Private notes, end-to-end encrypted.** Agents leave a note on a
  conversation for other agents in the workspace. The server stores it but
  must not be able to read it. Write `PROTOCOL.md`: who holds which key, what
  the server stores, and three attacks your scheme does **not** stop.
- **Tests** for the two or three pieces of logic most likely to be wrong.
- **Search** over messages with Elasticsearch, limited to the user's workspace.
- **Bonus: billing.** Per-seat subscriptions through Paybox. Scored separately
  (10 bonus points). See `BONUS_BILLING.md`. Last, if at all.

## The contract the check relies on

Keep these exactly as written. Everything else about your API is yours.

**A. `switchboard.json`** in the repository root holds the command that starts
your server from a clean clone after `install`. The check runs it itself.

```json
{ "install": "npm run scaffold:install", "start": "npm --prefix scaffold/server start", "health": "/healthz" }
```

**B. Configuration comes from the environment.** Your server listens on the
port in `PORT` and reads every URL and secret from the variables in
`.env.example`. Hard-coded ports or URLs will fail the check. The health path
answers `200` once the server is ready for traffic, and the check waits for that.

**C. Webhook path:** `POST /webhooks/pigeon`.

**D. Check endpoints**, protected by header `x-grader-token` equal to the env
var `GRADER_TOKEN`; without it, or with a wrong one, they answer `401`. They must go through the same code paths your UI uses.

| Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /__grader/reset` | Delete all application data, in MongoDB and Redis (login sessions may stay). Answer `200`. |
| `GET /__grader/snapshot` | Return what your system currently believes (shape below). |
| `POST /__grader/reply` `{ workspace, contact, text, client_ref }` | Send a reply to that contact as if an agent typed it, using the given `client_ref` with Pigeon. The contact may not have written yet: the reply still goes out and a conversation now exists. Answer `202` once it is safely stored. The same `client_ref` asked twice, even at the same instant, is one reply and both requests get `202`. A workspace that does not exist is a `4xx`. |
| `POST /__grader/claim` `{ workspace, contact, agent }` | Agent claims that contact's conversation. `200` if this agent now holds it, `409` if someone else does. The holder claiming again gets `200`. If the contact has not written yet, the claim creates the conversation. `agent` is an opaque id; do not look it up in the IdP. |

**E. Login and API**, used by level 5 and by your own frontend.

| Endpoint | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /auth/login` | Redirects the browser to the IdP (authorization code + PKCE). |
| `GET /auth/callback` | Finishes the login and sets a session cookie. |
| `GET /api/me` | `200 { "sub": "u_ben", "workspaces": [{ "id": "ws_acme", "role": "agent" }] }` with a session, `401` without. |
| `GET /api/conversations?workspace=<id>` | The inbox list, in any shape you like. `200` for a member of that workspace, `403` for a signed-in user who is not a member, `401` without a session. |

**F. WebSocket:** `GET /ws?workspace=<id>`, authenticated by the same session
cookie. Refuse the upgrade without a session, or for a workspace the user is
not a member of. Send JSON text frames. Every frame that reports a change
carries `seq`, an integer that only goes up within a workspace:

```json
{ "seq": 41, "type": "message.inbound", "contact": "+14155550101", "message_id": "pmsg_00001ab12" }
{ "seq": 42, "type": "message.status", "contact": "+14155550101", "client_ref": "<ref>", "status": "delivered" }
{ "seq": 43, "type": "conversation.assigned", "contact": "+14155550101", "assignee": "u_ben" }
```

Add any other fields you need. `GET /ws?workspace=<id>&after=41` first sends
every frame after 41 that the client missed, then continues live. With several
copies running, a browser connected to one copy must receive what another
copy processed.

The snapshot shape:

```json
{
  "workspaces": {
    "ws_acme": {
      "contacts": {
        "+14155550101": { "inbound": ["pmsg_00001ab12", "pmsg_00007cd34"], "assignee": "u_ben" }
      },
      "outbound": { "<client_ref>": "delivered" }
    }
  }
}
```

`inbound` is the list of Pigeon `message_id`s for that contact, in the order
your UI shows them, oldest first. `assignee` is who holds the conversation, or
`null`. `outbound` maps the `client_ref` of each message you sent to its
current status.

# Pigeon — provider contract

Base URL `http://localhost:4010`. Workspaces and API keys:

| Workspace | API key |
| --- | --- |
| `ws_acme` | `pk_acme_7d1f0a` |
| `ws_globex` | `pk_globex_c93b22` |

Webhook signing secret: `whsec_pigeon_dev`.

## Who is on the other end

Nobody real. Pigeon contains twelve simulated customers, six per workspace,
and a small set of canned texts. It picks one and posts it to you as if that
person had just written to the business. There is no customer app to build.
Customers do not answer your replies; they write on their own schedule.
Nothing you send goes anywhere: Pigeon records it and reports a status.

| Workspace | Simulated customers |
| --- | --- |
| `ws_acme` | +14155550101, +14155550102, +14155550103, +12125550104, +12125550105, +13035550106 |
| `ws_globex` | +442079460201, +442079460202, +442079460203, +4930901820204, +34600111205, +34600111206 |

## Webhooks Pigeon sends you

`POST <your url>` (default `http://localhost:4000/webhooks/pigeon`)

Headers:

- `x-pigeon-signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>` where `v1` is
  HMAC-SHA256 of `"<t>.<raw request body>"` with the signing secret.
- `x-pigeon-event-id: <event id>`

Body, a contact wrote in:

```json
{ "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.inbound", "workspace": "ws_acme",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:00.123Z",
  "data": { "message_id": "pmsg_...", "from": "+14155550101", "text": "Hi" } }
```

Body, status of a message you sent:

```json
{ "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.status", "workspace": "ws_acme",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:02.456Z",
  "data": { "message_id": "pm_...", "client_ref": "<yours>", "status": "sent" } }
```

`status` is `sent`, then `delivered` or `failed`.

What Pigeon promises, and what it does not:

- **At least once.** The same event can arrive several times.
- **No ordering.** Events can arrive in a different order than `occurred_at`.
  `delivered` can arrive before `sent`.
- **Retries.** If you do not answer `2xx` within 5 seconds, Pigeon sends the
  event again: six attempts in all, spread over about 22 seconds. After that
  it is gone. A server that is down for a few seconds therefore loses nothing,
  provided it never answers `2xx` for an event it has not safely stored.
- **Bursts.** Dozens of events in under a second happen.
- **The URL is public.** Anyone can post to it. Pigeon expects you to reject
  requests that are not genuinely from Pigeon, and requests whose timestamp is
  more than five minutes old, with `401`.

### How your endpoint must answer

| Request | Your answer |
| --- | --- |
| Signature missing, malformed, or not matching the raw body | `401`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Signature valid, timestamp more than five minutes old | `401` |
| Signature valid, timestamp up to five minutes old | Genuine. Slow networks exist. |
| Valid event, stored safely (or already stored earlier) | `2xx`, within 5 seconds |
| Valid signature, an event `type` you do not know | `2xx`. Pigeon adds event types without notice, and anything else makes it retry. |
| Valid signature, a status for a message you never sent | `2xx`, and ignore it |
| Valid signature, a body you cannot parse | `400`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Valid signature, a `workspace` you do not know | `2xx`, and ignore it |

## Sending a message

`POST /v1/messages` with `Authorization: Bearer <api key>`

```json
{ "to": "+14155550101", "text": "Hello", "client_ref": "<your id for this message>" }
```

`200 { "id": "pm_...", "status": "accepted" }`

- `Idempotency-Key` header: a repeated key returns the original response and
  does not send again.
- The limit is per workspace: a bucket of 8 sends that refills at 4 a second.
  Beyond it you get `429` with `Retry-After: <seconds>`. Requests sent before that time has
  passed are rejected and counted against you.
- `503` now and then.
- Sometimes Pigeon accepts and delivers a message but its HTTP response takes
  12 seconds. Your client will probably have given up by then.
- Now and then Pigeon is down altogether for a while: every send gets `503`
  until it recovers. A reply an agent sent in that window must still go out.

## While developing

```
# make a contact write to you now
curl -X POST localhost:4010/v1/simulate/inbound -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"workspace":"ws_acme","from":"+14155550101","text":"hello"}'

# force a failure on a send: timeout | 503 | 429
curl -X POST localhost:4010/v1/messages -H 'authorization: Bearer pk_acme_7d1f0a' \
  -H 'x-pigeon-force: timeout' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"to":"+14155550101","text":"hi","client_ref":"m1"}'

# run the traffic profile the check uses
curl -X POST localhost:4010/__admin/start -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"profile":"chaos"}'

# what Pigeon saw
curl localhost:4010/__admin/report

# take the send API down for 15 seconds
curl -X POST localhost:4010/__admin/outage -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"seconds":15}'
```

The same things as npm scripts: `npm run inbound`, `npm run chaos`, `npm run report`.

By default Pigeon also sends one message every 4 to 8 seconds ("drizzle") so
your inbox is never empty. `npm run quiet` stops that and `npm run drizzle`
turns it back on.

# Switchboard — build round

Build the first version of **Switchboard**, a shared team inbox. Customers
write to a business over a messaging provider. Support agents (people who work
at that business) log in, see conversations arrive in real time, reply, and
leave private notes for each other.

Several businesses (workspaces) use the same deployment. They must never see
each other's data.

**You will not finish everything below.** That is intended. Build the product
first, then make it survive: a small product that keeps working when the
network is bad, the process dies or a second copy is started beats a large one
that works only on the happy path.

Use any AI tools you like. You own every line you submit: in the follow-up
call we open your code, ask why it is the way it is, and debug it with you.

## The two hours

| Time | What |
| --- | --- |
| 0:00 – 0:10 | Read `START_HERE.md` and this brief. Start the services. |
| 0:10 – 1:50 | Build. Commit at least every 15 minutes. |
| 1:50 – 2:00 | Run the full check, push, make the repository public, send the form. See `SUBMISSION.md`. |

The form closes at 2:00. What counts is the commit you name in the form.

## How it fits together

```
simulated customers -> Pigeon :4010 --webhook POST--> YOUR SERVER --WebSocket--> YOUR REACT APP
        (given)          (given)                      (you build)                 (you build)

agent types a reply -> YOUR SERVER -> POST /v1/messages on Pigeon -> status webhooks back to you
```

You build the business side only. The customers are simulated and live inside
Pigeon; there is no customer app, and they do not answer your replies.

| Service | Port | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pigeon | 4010 | The messaging provider (simulated). Sends you webhooks, accepts your sends. Unreliable on purpose. See `PIGEON.md`. |
| Mock IdP | 4020 | OpenID Connect provider with five test users. Discovery at `/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Client id `switchboard-web`. PKCE (S256) is required. |
| MongoDB | 27017 | Real. |
| Redis | 6379 | Real. |
| Elasticsearch | 9200 | Real, optional: `npm run up:search`. |
| Paybox | 4030 | Simulated payment provider. Only for the bonus. See `PAYBOX.md`. |

`scaffold/` is an optional empty shell (Express + TypeScript server, Vite +
React app, already pointed at the services). It has no product code. Use it,
or delete it and bring your own Node stack; then change the `start` command in
`switchboard.json`.

## What to build

### The product
1. **Login.** Sign in through the IdP (authorization code + PKCE). A user's
   workspaces and roles come from the `workspaces` claim. Roles: `admin`, `agent`.
2. **Receive messages.** Accept Pigeon webhooks at `POST /webhooks/pigeon`.
   Pigeon is not a friendly network: read `PIGEON.md` before you write this.
3. **Inbox.** Conversations per contact, newest activity first, paginated.
   Open a conversation and read its messages in order. An agent can claim a
   conversation; two agents cannot both hold it. Close and reopen.
4. **Reply.** An agent replies and the message goes out through Pigeon. The
   agent sees its status: queued, sent, delivered, failed. A customer must
   never receive the same reply twice, and a reply must not be lost.
5. **Real time.** New messages, status changes and assignments appear without
   a refresh (WebSockets). A client that drops and reconnects misses nothing.
6. **Frontend.** A React app an agent could actually use for the above.

### Making it survive: the five levels
The automatic check has five levels. Each is worth points on its own. You can
run all of them yourself except level 4.

| Level | Situation | Points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | One copy of your server. Webhooks arrive duplicated, out of order, forged and replayed. Pigeon rate-limits you, answers slowly, and goes down for a while. Six agents claim one conversation in the same instant. | 24 |
| 2 | Your server is **killed without warning** (`kill -9`) and started again a few seconds later: once in the middle of a flood of webhooks, once just after it accepted a batch of replies. Nothing may be lost, duplicated or sent twice. | 14 |
| 3 | **Several copies** of your server run behind a load balancer and share MongoDB and Redis. Everything in level 1 must still hold, the rate limit is per workspace and not per copy, and when one copy dies for good the others finish its work within 60 seconds. | 22 |

| 5 | **Login, tenant isolation and real time**, with several copies running. The check signs in through the IdP as a browser would, calls your API as a user of one workspace, and listens on your WebSocket while customers write. | 15 |

### Also valued (reviewed, not checked automatically)
- **Private notes, end-to-end encrypted.** Agents leave a note on a
  conversation for other agents in the workspace. The server stores it but
  must not be able to read it. Write `PROTOCOL.md`: who holds which key, what
  the server stores, and three attacks your scheme does **not** stop.

- **Search** over messages with Elasticsearch, limited to the user's workspace.

- `switchboard.json`: correct `install` and `start` commands.
- `DECISIONS.md`, half a page: what you built, what you cut and why, what you
  assumed where this brief is silent, and **what you know is still wrong**.
  An honest "level 3 loses replies when a copy dies; I think it is the lock"
  is worth more than silence.
- `CHECK_REPORT.json`: written by your last `npm run check:full`.
- `ai-logs/`: exported transcripts of every AI session you used. Required:
  without them the AI part scores 0 and your submission goes to manual review.

This brief leaves several things unsaid. When you hit one, decide, write the
decision in `DECISIONS.md`, and move on. Questions go in the question channel;
answers go to everyone.
# Pigeon — provider contract

Base URL `http://localhost:4010`. Workspaces and API keys:

| Workspace | API key |
| --- | --- |
| `ws_acme` | `pk_acme_7d1f0a` |
| `ws_globex` | `pk_globex_c93b22` |

Webhook signing secret: `whsec_pigeon_dev`.

## Who is on the other end

Nobody real. Pigeon contains twelve simulated customers, six per workspace,
and a small set of canned texts. It picks one and posts it to you as if that
person had just written to the business. There is no customer app to build.
Customers do not answer your replies; they write on their own schedule.
Nothing you send goes anywhere: Pigeon records it and reports a status.

| Workspace | Simulated customers |
| --- | --- |
| `ws_acme` | +14155550101, +14155550102, +14155550103, +12125550104, +12125550105, +13035550106 |
| `ws_globex` | +442079460201, +442079460202, +442079460203, +4930901820204, +34600111205, +34600111206 |

## Webhooks Pigeon sends you

`POST <your url>` (default `http://localhost:4000/webhooks/pigeon`)

Headers:

- `x-pigeon-signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>` where `v1` is
  HMAC-SHA256 of `"<t>.<raw request body>"` with the signing secret.
- `x-pigeon-event-id: <event id>`

Body, a contact wrote in:

```json
{ "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.inbound", "workspace": "ws_acme",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:00.123Z",
  "data": { "message_id": "pmsg_...", "from": "+14155550101", "text": "Hi" } }
```

Body, status of a message you sent:

```json
{ "id": "evt_...", "type": "message.status", "workspace": "ws_acme",
  "occurred_at": "2026-11-18T09:30:02.456Z",
  "data": { "message_id": "pm_...", "client_ref": "<yours>", "status": "sent" } }
```

`status` is `sent`, then `delivered` or `failed`.

What Pigeon promises, and what it does not:

- **At least once.** The same event can arrive several times.
- **No ordering.** Events can arrive in a different order than `occurred_at`.
  `delivered` can arrive before `sent`.
- **Retries.** If you do not answer `2xx` within 5 seconds, Pigeon sends the
  event again: six attempts in all, spread over about 22 seconds. After that
  it is gone. A server that is down for a few seconds therefore loses nothing,
  provided it never answers `2xx` for an event it has not safely stored.
- **Bursts.** Dozens of events in under a second happen.
- **The URL is public.** Anyone can post to it. Pigeon expects you to reject
  requests that are not genuinely from Pigeon, and requests whose timestamp is
  more than five minutes old, with `401`.

### How your endpoint must answer

| Request | Your answer |
| --- | --- |
| Signature missing, malformed, or not matching the raw body | `401`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Signature valid, timestamp more than five minutes old | `401` |
| Signature valid, timestamp up to five minutes old | Genuine. Slow networks exist. |
| Valid event, stored safely (or already stored earlier) | `2xx`, within 5 seconds |
| Valid signature, an event `type` you do not know | `2xx`. Pigeon adds event types without notice, and anything else makes it retry. |
| Valid signature, a status for a message you never sent | `2xx`, and ignore it |
| Valid signature, a body you cannot parse | `400`. Never a `5xx`. |
| Valid signature, a `workspace` you do not know | `2xx`, and ignore it |

## Sending a message

`POST /v1/messages` with `Authorization: Bearer <api key>`

```json
{ "to": "+14155550101", "text": "Hello", "client_ref": "<your id for this message>" }
```

`200 { "id": "pm_...", "status": "accepted" }`

- `Idempotency-Key` header: a repeated key returns the original response and
  does not send again.
- The limit is per workspace: a bucket of 8 sends that refills at 4 a second.
  Beyond it you get `429` with `Retry-After: <seconds>`. Requests sent before that time has
  passed are rejected and counted against you.
- `503` now and then.
- Sometimes Pigeon accepts and delivers a message but its HTTP response takes
  12 seconds. Your client will probably have given up by then.
- Now and then Pigeon is down altogether for a while: every send gets `503`
  until it recovers. A reply an agent sent in that window must still go out.

## While developing

```
# make a contact write to you now
curl -X POST localhost:4010/v1/simulate/inbound -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"workspace":"ws_acme","from":"+14155550101","text":"hello"}'

# force a failure on a send: timeout | 503 | 429
curl -X POST localhost:4010/v1/messages -H 'authorization: Bearer pk_acme_7d1f0a' \
  -H 'x-pigeon-force: timeout' -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"to":"+14155550101","text":"hi","client_ref":"m1"}'

# run the traffic profile the check uses
curl -X POST localhost:4010/__admin/start -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"profile":"chaos"}'

# what Pigeon saw
curl localhost:4010/__admin/report

# take the send API down for 15 seconds
curl -X POST localhost:4010/__admin/outage -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"seconds":15}'
```

The same things as npm scripts: `npm run inbound`, `npm run chaos`, `npm run report`.

By default Pigeon also sends one message every 4 to 8 seconds ("drizzle") so
your inbox is never empty. `npm run quiet` stops that and `npm run drizzle`
turns it back on.

content.text:
Setup is done (6:08 PM). I made the `starter` commit, `npm run up` and `npm run doctor` both pass, and I installed the scaffold because it fits. I also added `.DS_Store` to `.gitignore`.

## What the brief asks for
**Switchboard** is a shared team inbox that several businesses (workspaces) use. Customer messages come in as webhooks from **Pigeon**, the messaging provider. Support agents, meaning people who work at the business and not AI bots, log in through the mock IdP. They see conversations update live, claim a conversation, reply through Pigeon and see each reply's status. One workspace must never see another's data.

**Fixed contract (the check depends on it):** `switchboard.json`, a server listening on `PORT` with `/healthz`, `POST /webhooks/pigeon`, the `/__grader/{reset,snapshot,reply,claim}` endpoints behind `x-grader-token`, `/auth/login`, `/auth/callback`, `/api/me`, `/api/conversations?workspace=`, and `/ws?workspace=&after=` sending frames with a `seq` that only goes up within a workspace.

## How it's scored (85 points from the check, plus 15)
| Level | What happens | Pts |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Duplicated, out-of-order, forged and replayed webhooks; 429 / 503 / 12 s slow responses / outages; 6 agents claim one conversation at once | 24 |
| 2 | Server killed with `kill -9` during a webhook flood, and again right after it accepted replies | 14 |
| 3 | Several copies sharing Mongo and Redis; rate limit per workspace; a copy that dies for good has its work finished by the others within 60 s | 22 |
| 4 | The written rules in PIGEON.md (we can't run this level ourselves) | 10 |
| 5 | Login, tenant isolation, WebSocket with replay, all with several copies running | 15 |

The other 15 points cover security, code quality and tests, the frontend and what was cut, and the `ai-logs/` exports. Encrypted notes, search and billing are optional extras.

## Traps
- **The check picks `PORT`** (4001, 4002, …) and runs a load balancer on 4000. Nothing may be hard-coded.
- **`npm run check` wipes application data and starts the server itself.** We have to stop the dev server before running it.
- **"Agent" means a human support agent.** No bot is needed.
- **Webhook rules:** forged, missing or bad signature, or a timestamp older than 5 min → `401`, never a `5xx`. Body that won't parse → `400`. Unknown type, unknown workspace, or a status for a message we never sent → `2xx`. Answer `2xx` only **after** the event is stored.
- **Reply status only moves forward.** `delivered` can arrive before `sent`, so a late `sent` must not overwrite it.

## Proposed design (your call; this is what you'll defend in the interview)
- **Webhook:** verify the signature over the raw body, then do an idempotent upsert with a unique index on `(workspace, message_id)`. Answer `200` only after the write. Messages are shown in `occurred_at` order.
- **Replies (outbox):** save `{client_ref, status: queued}` with a unique index on `(workspace, client_ref)`, then answer `202`. A worker in every copy picks up queued replies with a lease: one `findOneAndUpdate` sets `lockedUntil`. If a copy dies, its lease runs out and another copy takes the work. We send with `Idempotency-Key = client_ref`, so a retry can never send twice. The rate limit is a token bucket in Redis per workspace, and it follows Pigeon's `Retry-After`.
- **Claim:** a single conditional `findOneAndUpdate` (`assignee` is `null` or already this agent) plus a unique index. That is atomic, so only one of six simultaneous claims wins.
- **Real time:** Redis `INCR` gives each workspace its `seq`. Every frame is stored in Mongo so `after=` can replay missed ones. Redis pub/sub carries frames between copies.
- **Auth:** PKCE login done by hand, with sessions stored in Redis so every copy shares them.

## Proposed order
1. **(about 40 min)** Webhook, reset, snapshot, grader reply and claim, outbox worker, then run `npm run check` (level 1). We commit and run the check from this step on.
2. **(about 25 min)** Auth, `/api/me`, `/api/conversations`, then WebSocket with `seq` and replay (level 5).
3. **(about 20 min)** Harden for levels 2 and 3 (leases, the shared rate limiter), then run `check:full`.
4. **(about 15 min)** A minimal React inbox: list, thread, reply, claim, live updates.
5. **At the end:** README, DECISIONS.md, `ai-logs/`.

**Cut:** encrypted notes, Elasticsearch search and billing, unless time is left. Maybe one test file for the outbox and the claim logic.

I'll wait for your go-ahead before building anything.

# Switchboard

A shared team inbox. Customer messages arrive as Pigeon webhooks. Support agents sign in through the IdP, see conversations update live, claim a conversation, reply through Pigeon and see each reply's status (queued, sent, delivered or failed).

Stack: Node 22 + TypeScript (Express, `ws`), MongoDB, Redis, React (Vite). Both live under `scaffold/`.

## Run from a clean clone

Requirements: Node 22 or newer, and Docker.

```bash
npm run up                 # MongoDB, Redis, Pigeon, IdP (Docker)
npm run doctor             # every port should PASS
npm run scaffold:install   # server + web dependencies
npm run scaffold:server    # API on http://localhost:4000 (PORT overrides)
npm run scaffold:web       # React app on http://localhost:5173
```

Open http://localhost:5173 and click **Sign in**. The IdP lists its test users (for example Ben in `ws_acme`, or Eli in both workspaces).

All configuration comes from the environment (see `.env.example`). The defaults match the harness, so no `.env` file is needed.

## Check and tests

```bash
npm run check:full                 # stop your dev server first: it starts its own and wipes data
npm --prefix scaffold/server test  # unit/integration tests (uses db switchboard_test)
```

## Layout (`scaffold/server/src`)

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `index.ts` | Routes: webhook, `/__grader/*`, `/auth/*`, `/api/*`, health and boot |
| `webhook.ts` | Signature and timestamp check on the raw body, idempotent store, forward-only status |
| `outbox.ts` | Reply outbox in MongoDB, leased worker in every copy, Redis token bucket and Retry-After cool-off per workspace |
| `inbox.ts` | Atomic claim, list (keyset pagination), thread, snapshot, reset |
| `realtime.ts` | `seq` per workspace (Redis INCR), frames stored in MongoDB, Redis pub/sub between copies, replay with `after=` |
| `auth.ts` | OIDC code flow + PKCE; login state and sessions in Redis (httpOnly cookie) |
| `store.ts` | Collections, indexes and deterministic ids |

See `DECISIONS.md` for what was built, what was cut and what is still wrong.

# Switchboard

A shared team inbox. Customer messages arrive as Pigeon webhooks. Support agents sign in through the IdP, see conversations update live, claim a conversation, reply through Pigeon and see each reply's status (queued, sent, delivered or failed).

Stack: Node 22 + TypeScript (Express, `ws`), MongoDB, Redis, React (Vite). Both live under `scaffold/`.

## Run from a clean clone

Requirements: Node 22 or newer, and Docker.

```bash
npm run up                 # MongoDB, Redis, Pigeon, IdP (Docker)
npm run doctor             # every port should PASS
npm run scaffold:install   # server + web dependencies
npm run scaffold:server    # API on http://localhost:4000 (PORT overrides)
npm run scaffold:web       # React app on http://localhost:5173
```

Open http://localhost:5173 and click **Sign in**. The IdP lists its test users (for example Ben in `ws_acme`, or Eli in both workspaces).

All configuration comes from the environment (see `.env.example`). The defaults match the harness, so no `.env` file is needed.

## Check and tests

```bash
npm run check:full                 # stop your dev server first: it starts its own and wipes data
npm --prefix scaffold/server test  # unit/integration tests (uses db switchboard_test)
```

## Layout (`scaffold/server/src`)

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `index.ts` | Routes: webhook, `/__grader/*`, `/auth/*`, `/api/*`, health and boot |
| `webhook.ts` | Signature and timestamp check on the raw body, idempotent store, forward-only status |
| `outbox.ts` | Reply outbox in MongoDB, leased worker in every copy, Redis token bucket and Retry-After cool-off per workspace |
| `inbox.ts` | Atomic claim, list (keyset pagination), thread, snapshot, reset |
| `realtime.ts` | `seq` per workspace (Redis INCR), frames stored in MongoDB, Redis pub/sub between copies, replay with `after=` |
| `auth.ts` | OIDC code flow + PKCE; login state and sessions in Redis (httpOnly cookie) |
| `store.ts` | Collections, indexes and deterministic ids |

See `DECISIONS.md` for what was built, what was cut and what is still wrong.

# Decisions

## Built
- **Webhook**: HMAC check on the raw body, a ±5 min timestamp window, then an idempotent insert keyed by `workspace:message_id`. We answer `2xx` only after MongoDB has the write; if storage fails we answer `503` and Pigeon retries. Unknown type or unknown workspace → `200` (ignored); unparseable body → `400`; bad or missing signature → `401`.
- **Replies**: a transactional outbox in MongoDB keyed by `workspace:client_ref`, so the same ref twice is one row. Every server copy runs a worker that takes a job with a 20 s lease. If a copy dies, another takes the job once the lease runs out (well inside 60 s). Every send carries `Idempotency-Key = workspace:client_ref`, so retrying after a timeout or crash never sends twice. Rate limit: one Redis token bucket per workspace, shared by all copies (6 burst, 3/s, deliberately below Pigeon's 8 / 4/s), plus a shared cool-off key set from `Retry-After`; a 5xx also cools the workspace off for 1 s.
- **Status** only moves forward (`rank` condition in the update), so `delivered` arriving before `sent` holds. A status for a `client_ref` we never sent is ignored.
- **Claim** is one conditional upsert (`assignee` is null or me); the loser of the race hits a duplicate key → `409`.
- **Real time**: `seq` comes from Redis `INCR` per workspace; frames are stored in MongoDB; a Redis publish wakes every copy. Each socket *pulls* `seq > last` from MongoDB in order, so it never reorders, and `after=N` replay is the same code path.
- **Auth**: OIDC code + PKCE, with state and verifier in Redis (login and callback may land on different copies). Sessions live in Redis behind an httpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie. Workspaces and roles come from `/userinfo`.
- **Frontend**: login, workspace switcher, open/closed/all filter, paginated list, thread, claim/release/close/reopen, reply with live status, auto-reconnecting socket with `after=`. Replies use a `client_ref` made in the browser, so a retried POST is still one reply.

## Cut, and why
- **Encrypted notes, search, billing**: lower value per minute than the 85 points from the check. No `PROTOCOL.md`.
- **Admin vs agent**: roles are stored and shown, but nothing is admin-only yet.

## Assumptions where the brief is silent
- A new inbound message reopens a closed conversation; a reply does not.
- `POST /__grader/reply` to an unknown workspace → `404`; missing fields → `400`.
- Messages in a thread are ordered by `occurred_at` (inbound) and send time (our replies).
- Any other Pigeon 4xx on send (not 429) is final → `failed`.

## Known to be wrong or weak
- **Lost status frames on crash**: if the process dies between storing a status or claim and storing its realtime frame, that frame is lost (the data is right; only the live push is missing). Inbound messages are covered by a `framed` flag; status and claim frames are not.
- **Gap skip**: a socket waits 2 s for a missing `seq` (taken by INCR but not yet stored), then skips it. A frame stored later than that is never pushed to that socket.
- **`seq` lives in Redis**: if Redis loses its data, `seq` restarts and clients reconnecting with an old `after=` miss frames. It could be rebuilt from the highest `seq` in MongoDB at boot.
- **No CSRF token**: we rely on SameSite=Lax plus JSON bodies. The id_token signature is not verified; identity comes from userinfo over the server-to-server channel.
- After `/__grader/reset`, already-open sockets keep their old `last` and stay silent until they reconnect.

The private repo is [anjaliSilawat/switchboard](https://github.com/anjaliSilawat/switchboard), and every commit so far is pushed (the last one at 6:17 PM).

**What's built:**
- **Server**, in `scaffold/server/src`:
  - **Webhook:** checks the signature on the raw request body before reading it. It answers `2xx` only after MongoDB has saved the message, and a duplicate message is stored once.
  - **Reply queue:** a reply is saved in MongoDB first. Each server copy runs a worker that sends queued replies, holding each job for at most 20 seconds so another copy takes over if one dies. Sends use `Idempotency-Key`, so a retry never reaches the customer twice. The rate limit is one Redis bucket per workspace, shared by all copies.
  - **Claim:** a single conditional database update, so only one of six simultaneous claims can win.
  - **Live updates:** the `seq` number comes from Redis. Frames are stored in MongoDB so a reconnecting client can replay what it missed with `after=`.
  - **Login:** PKCE, with sessions stored in Redis so every copy can read them.
- **React app:** sign-in, workspace switcher, inbox with "load more" paging, conversation view, reply with live status, claim/release/close/reopen, and a WebSocket that reconnects on its own.
- **Tests:** 3, all passing (`npm --prefix scaffold/server test`). They cover the signature check, the six-way claim race, and a late `sent` not overwriting `delivered`.
- **Docs:** `README.md` and a draft `DECISIONS.md`. The draft already lists the weak spots: a status update's live frame can be lost if the server crashes at the wrong moment, a socket skips a missing `seq` after waiting 2 seconds, `seq` lives only in Redis, and there is no CSRF token.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Switchboard

A shared team inbox. Customer messages arrive as Pigeon webhooks. Support agents sign in through the IdP, see conversations update live, claim a conversation, reply through Pigeon and see each reply's status (queued, sent, delivered or failed).

Stack: Node 22 + TypeScript (Express, `ws`), MongoDB, Redis, React (Vite). Both live under `scaffold/`.

## Run from a clean clone

Requirements: Node 22 or newer, and Docker.

```bash
npm run up                 # MongoDB, Redis, Pigeon, IdP (Docker)
npm run doctor             # every port should PASS
npm run scaffold:install   # server + web dependencies
npm run scaffold:server    # API on http://localhost:4000 (PORT overrides)
npm run scaffold:web       # React app on http://localhost:5173
```

Open http://localhost:5173 and click **Sign in**. The IdP lists its test users (for example Ben in `ws_acme`, or Eli in both workspaces).

All configuration comes from the environment (see `.env.example`). The defaults match the harness, so no `.env` file is needed.

## Check and tests

```bash
npm run check:full                 # stop your dev server first: it starts its own and wipes data
npm --prefix scaffold/server test  # unit/integration tests (uses db switchboard_test)
```

## Layout (`scaffold/server/src`)

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `index.ts` | Routes: webhook, `/__grader/*`, `/auth/*`, `/api/*`, health and boot |
| `webhook.ts` | Signature and timestamp check on the raw body, idempotent store, forward-only status |
| `outbox.ts` | Reply outbox in MongoDB, leased worker in every copy, Redis token bucket and Retry-After cool-off per workspace |
| `inbox.ts` | Atomic claim, list (keyset pagination), thread, snapshot, reset |
| `realtime.ts` | `seq` per workspace (Redis INCR), frames stored in MongoDB, Redis pub/sub between copies, replay with `after=` |
| `auth.ts` | OIDC code flow + PKCE; login state and sessions in Redis (httpOnly cookie) |
| `store.ts` | Collections, indexes and deterministic ids |

See `DECISIONS.md` for what was built, what was cut and what is still wrong.

# Private notes: how the encryption works

Goal: agents of a workspace can leave notes on a conversation for each other, and the server stores the notes but **cannot read them**.

## Who holds which key

- The agents of a workspace agree on a **team passphrase** outside the app (for example, an admin tells the team in person or in their password manager). The passphrase is never sent to the server.
- Each agent's browser turns the passphrase into a key:
  `key = PBKDF2-SHA256(passphrase, salt = "switchboard-notes:" + workspaceId, 200 000 rounds) → AES-256-GCM key`
  (`scaffold/web/src/notesCrypto.ts`). The key exists only in that browser tab's memory and is gone after a reload.
- The server holds **no key**.

## What the server stores (`notes` collection)

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `workspace`, `contact` | Which conversation the note belongs to (plain) |
| `author`, `authorName` | Who wrote it (plain, taken from the session, not from the browser) |
| `createdAt` | When (plain) |
| `iv` | 12 random bytes, new for every note (base64) |
| `ciphertext` | AES-GCM encryption of the note text, including the auth tag (base64) |

Reading a note: the browser downloads `ciphertext` and `iv` and decrypts them with its key. If the passphrase is wrong, AES-GCM decryption fails and the UI says "Can not decrypt".

## Three attacks this scheme does NOT stop

1. **A malicious or hacked server changes the JavaScript it serves.** The same server delivers the app, so it could ship code that sends the passphrase or the decrypted notes back to it. End-to-end encryption in a web app trusts whoever serves the code.
2. **Guessing a weak passphrase offline.** Someone who steals the database (or the server operator) has the ciphertext and knows the salt (the workspace id). PBKDF2 makes each guess slow, but a short or common passphrase can still be found.
3. **A removed agent keeps access.** There is no key rotation or per-user keys. An agent who leaves still knows the passphrase and can read every old and new note (if they can get the ciphertext). Changing the passphrase also makes old notes unreadable for everyone.

Also not protected: the metadata (who wrote a note, when, on which conversation) is plain text, and the server can delete notes or hide some of them from a user without anyone noticing.

attachment.snippet:
4	- **Webhook**: HMAC check on the raw body, a ±5 min timestamp window, then an idempotent insert keyed by `workspace:message_id`. We answer `2xx` only after MongoDB has the write; if storage fails we answer `503` and Pigeon retries. Unknown type or unknown workspace → `200` (ignored); unparseable body → `400`; bad or missing signature → `401`.
5	- **Replies**: a transactional outbox in MongoDB keyed by `workspace:client_ref`, so the same ref twice is one row. Every server copy runs a worker that takes a job with a 20 s lease. If a copy dies, another takes the job once the lease runs out (well inside 60 s). Every send carries `Idempotency-Key = workspace:client_ref`, so retrying after a timeout or crash never sends twice. Rate limit: one Redis token bucket per workspace, shared by all copies (6 burst, 3/s, deliberately below Pigeon's 8 / 4/s), plus a shared cool-off key set from `Retry-After`; a 5xx also cools the workspace off for 1 s.
6	- **Status** only moves forward (`rank` condition in the update), so `delivered` arriving before `sent` holds. A status for a `client_ref` we never sent is ignored.
7	- **Claim** is one conditional upsert (`assignee` is null or me); the loser of the race hits a duplicate key → `409`.
8	- **Real time**: `seq` comes from Redis `INCR` per workspace; frames are stored in MongoDB; a Redis publish wakes every copy. Each socket *pulls* `seq > last` from MongoDB in order, so it never reorders, and `after=N` replay is the same code path.
9	- **Auth**: OIDC code + PKCE, with state and verifier in Redis (login and callback may land on different copies). Sessions live in Redis behind an httpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie. Workspaces and roles come from `/userinfo`.
10	- **Frontend**: login, workspace switcher, open/closed/all filter, paginated list, thread, claim/release/close/reopen, reply with live status, auto-reconnecting socket with `after=`. Replies use a `client_ref` made in the browser, so a retried POST is still one reply.
11	
12	- **Private notes, end-to-end encrypted**: each browser derives an AES-GCM key from a team passphrase (PBKDF2). The server stores only ciphertext + iv. See `PROTOCOL.md`.
13	- **One origin**: the API server also serves the built React app, so `http://localhost:4000` is the whole product.
14	
15	## Cut, and why
16	- **Search and billing**: lower value per minute than making the check pass under failure.
17	- **Notes key management**: one shared passphrase per workspace, no rotation or per-user keys (simple to explain and build in the time).
18	- **Admin vs agent**: roles are stored and shown, but nothing is admin-only yet.
19	
20	## Assumptions where the brief is silent
21	- A new inbound message reopens a closed conversation; a reply does not.
22	- `POST /__grader/reply` to an unknown workspace → `404`; missing fields → `400`.
23	- Messages in a thread are ordered by `occurred_at` (inbound) and send time (our replies).
24	- Any other Pigeon 4xx on send (not 429) is final → `failed`.

9	- **Auth**: OIDC code + PKCE, with state and verifier in Redis (login and callback may land on different copies). Sessions live in Redis behind an httpOnly SameSite=Lax cookie. Workspaces and roles come from `/userinfo`.
10	- **Frontend**: login, workspace switcher, open/closed/all filter, paginated list, thread, claim/release/close/reopen, reply with live status, auto-reconnecting socket with `after=`. Replies use a `client_ref` made in the browser, so a retried POST is still one reply.
11	
12	- **Private notes, end-to-end encrypted**: each browser derives an AES-GCM key from a team passphrase (PBKDF2). The server stores only ciphertext + iv. See `PROTOCOL.md`.
13	- **One origin**: the API server also serves the built React app, so `http://localhost:4000` is the whole product.
14	
15	## Cut, and why
16	- **Search and billing**: lower value per minute than making the check pass under failure.
17	- **Notes key management**: one shared passphrase per workspace, no rotation or per-user keys (simple to explain and build in the time).
18	- **Admin vs agent**: roles are stored and shown, but nothing is admin-only yet.
19	
20	## Assumptions where the brief is silent
21	- A new inbound message reopens a closed conversation; a reply does not.
22	- `POST /__grader/reply` to an unknown workspace → `404`; missing fields → `400`.
23	- Messages in a thread are ordered by `occurred_at` (inbound) and send time (our replies).
24	- Any other Pigeon 4xx on send (not 429) is final → `failed`.
25	
</system-reminder>

content.text:
The encrypted notes and the new UI are done, and the check still scores **75/75**. Everything is pushed. The app is running at **http://localhost:4000**, so you can open it in your browser and then look at the code in VS Code.

**New in the app:**
- **Login page:** a centered card on a gradient background, with a "Sign in" button and a short feature list.
- **Top bar:** dark, with the logo, workspace switcher, an admin/agent badge, and your name with initials.
- **Inbox:** Open / Closed / All tabs and a blinking green "Live" dot. Each conversation shows a coloured tag for who holds it: "Unassigned" (yellow), "You" (green), or the teammate's real name, e.g. "Ben Ortiz" instead of "u_ben".
- **Chat:** customer messages on the left, your replies in purple on the right, with ⏳ queued, ✓ sent, ✓✓ delivered and ⚠ failed.
- **🔒 Private notes** panel on the right: enter a team passphrase (at least 8 characters, for example `acme-team-notes`), then write notes. I checked MongoDB, and it stores only unreadable text like `rNmLF9vuqFl7/Jum…`. The server can't read the notes.

**Code, kept simple so you can explain it:** the web app is now small files, each with one job, and plain-English comments.

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `scaffold/web/src/api.ts` | fetch helper and data types |
| `scaffold/web/src/useLiveUpdates.ts` | WebSocket that reconnects and replays what it missed |
| `scaffold/web/src/notesCrypto.ts` | encryption: about 40 lines using the browser's built-in crypto |
| `scaffold/web/src/components/` | `LoginPage`, `Inbox`, `ConversationView`, `NotesPanel` |
| `scaffold/web/src/styles.css` | one CSS file with colour variables, no UI library |

**Docs:** `PROTOCOL.md` explains who holds the key, what the server stores, and three attacks the scheme does not stop. `DECISIONS.md` now records the check results.

**Checks:** I ran the full check after the changes and got 75/75. I also ran a harder version, with 3 server copies, twice the traffic and a 15-second Pigeon outage, which is closer to what the graders run. That also scored 75/75.

I didn't open your other projects. I kept the code at a level you can explain line by line.

Two points that may come up in the interview:
- **Notes:** "The key is made from a team passphrase in the browser, so the server only ever gets encrypted bytes."
- **Replies:** "Each reply gets an id in the browser, so if the request is retried the server knows it's the same reply and never sends it twice."

Time is 6:42 PM. Before 7:50, `ai-logs/` still has to be exported, and any other AI sessions you used today need to be in there too.

+.composer input:focus, .field:focus { border-color: var(--accent); box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px var(--accent-soft); background: white; }
+.empty { height: 100%; display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; justify-content: center; text-align: center; padding: 24px; }
+.empty-art span { position: absolute; height: 26px; border-radius: 12px; box-shadow: var(--shadow); }
+.empty-art span:nth-child(1) { left: 0; top: 0; width: 62px; background: white; }
+.empty-art span:nth-child(2) { right: 0; top: 22px; width: 54px; background: var(--ink); }
+.empty-art span:nth-child(3) { left: 10px; top: 44px; width: 40px; background: var(--accent); }
-.notes { width: 290px; flex: none; background: #fffdf5; border-left: 1px solid var(--border); display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
-.notes-head { padding: 14px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--border); display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 2px; font-weight: 700; }
-.unlock, .note-form { padding: 14px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 8px; }
-.unlock input, .note-form textarea { padding: 9px 12px; border: 1px solid var(--border); border-radius: 8px; outline: none; resize: vertical; }
-.note-list { flex: 1; overflow-y: auto; padding: 14px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 8px; }
-.note { background: var(--amber-soft); border: 1px solid #f3e2a9; border-radius: 10px; padding: 10px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 4px; white-space: pre-wrap; }
+.notes { width: 300px; flex: none; background: var(--panel); border-left: 1px solid var(--line); display: flex; flex-direction: column; }
+.notes-head { padding: 14px 16px; height: 68px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line); display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: center; }
+.notes-head strong { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px; }
+.lock { width: 18px; height: 18px; border-radius: 5px; background: var(--ink); display: inline-grid; place-items: center; color: white; font-size: 10px; }
+.unlock, .note-form { padding: 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 10px; }
+.unlock-art { width: 48px; height: 48px; border-radius: 14px; background: var(--sand-soft); display: grid; place-items: center; font-size: 22px; margin: 0 auto 4px; }
+.field { padding: 10px 12px; border: 1px solid var(--line); border-radius: 10px; outline: none; resize: vertical; background: var(--paper); }
+.note-list { flex: 1; overflow-y: auto; padding: 16px; display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 10px; }
+.note { background: #fff6d8; border-radius: 4px 12px 12px 12px; padding: 11px 12px; white-space: pre-wrap; box-shadow: 0 1px 0 #f0e2b0; }

content.text:
The new design is live at **http://localhost:4000**. Refresh the page to see it. It's committed and pushed (6:46 PM).

**What changed:**
- **Login page** is now split in two:
  - **Left:** a dark navy panel with a small example conversation (customer message, a private note, a delivered reply), a large serif headline and a soft coral glow.
  - **Right:** a clean "Welcome back" card with a coral button and three numbered steps.
- **Colours:** warm off-white background, deep navy, and one coral accent. I dropped the generic purple gradients and emoji icons that make apps look AI-made.
- **Fonts:** Manrope for the interface and Fraunces (a serif) for headings.
- **Top bar:** navy, with a combined workspace switcher and role badge, and your name with a coloured avatar.
- **Inbox:** an "Inbox" heading, a green "Live" badge that pulses, and segmented Open / Closed / All tabs. Each customer gets their own avatar colour. The selected row has a coral marker on its left edge, and status tags have a coloured dot.
- **Chat:** a beige background with a fine dot pattern. Customer bubbles are white, your replies are navy, and statuses show as ◷ queued, ✓ sent, and ✓✓ delivered in teal. A "Today" label appears where the day changes.
- **Empty states:** "Pick a conversation" has a small illustration made of three coloured bubbles.
- **Notes panel:** a key icon on the unlock screen, and notes shown as yellow sticky notes.

The code stays simple. It's still one CSS file with the colours as variables at the top. The only new file is `scaffold/web/src/avatar.ts`, about 15 lines: it picks the same colour for the same phone number every time.

I checked the login page and the inbox in the browser at desktop size. Only frontend files changed, but I haven't re-run the check since the redesign; I'll run `check:full` once more before submitting so `CHECK_REPORT.json` matches the final commit.

Refresh `localhost:4000`. The big empty area is no longer blank, and new customer messages are arriving again.

## What I fixed

**The plain white page with 5 names (Mock identity provider).** This page is **not ours**. It's the login simulator the assessment gives us (`localhost:4020`, the `idp/` folder). In a real company this would be Google or Microsoft's login page. The graders run their own copy, so we must not change it. Interview line: *"That's the identity provider; my app only redirects to it and gets the user back."*

**The empty middle area.** It now says "Hi Asha, pick a conversation" and shows 3 counters: **Open**, **Waiting for someone** (no one has claimed it) and **Assigned to you**.

**Inbox was nearly empty.** `npm run check` deletes all data and pauses the fake customers. I turned them back on (`npm run drizzle`), so a new message comes in every few seconds. The "level 5" messages you saw were test messages left over from the check.

## What Claim, Release, Close and Open mean

Picture a real support team: 5 agents, one shared inbox.

| Button / tab | Meaning | Why it exists |
|---|---|---|
| **Claim** | "I'll handle this customer." Your name goes on the conversation. | So two agents never reply to the same customer. If Ben has claimed it, Asha's Claim button is greyed out. The server allows only one owner, even if 6 people click at the same moment. |
| **Release** | "I'm not handling this anymore." It goes back to unassigned. | Someone else can pick it up. |
| **Close** | "This issue is solved." It moves to the **Closed** tab. | Keeps the Open list short. |
| **Reopen** | Brings a closed conversation back to Open. | If the customer writes again, it **reopens by itself**. That's why +14155550101 is back in Open. |
| **Open / Closed / All** tabs | Filters for the list on the left. | |

## The project in brief

**Switchboard** is a shared support inbox for businesses, a simple version of Intercom or WhatsApp Business for teams.

1. **A customer sends a message.** The provider (Pigeon) sends it to our server as a **webhook**. We check its **signature**, so fake messages are rejected, save it in **MongoDB**, and only then reply "OK". If our server crashes before saving, Pigeon sends it again, so nothing is lost.
2. **The agent sees it instantly** through a **WebSocket**. Every update has a number (`seq`). If the internet drops, the browser reconnects and says "send me everything after number 41", so nothing is missed.
3. **The agent claims the conversation and replies.** The reply is saved first with status **queued**, then a background worker sends it to Pigeon. The status then changes **sent → delivered** on screen.
4. **Reliability:**
   - The same reply is never sent twice: each reply has a unique id that Pigeon also checks.
   - We respect Pigeon's rate limit, with one shared counter in **Redis**.
   - If a server copy dies, another copy finishes its work.
5. **Login** goes through the identity provider (OAuth with PKCE). Each user only sees their own **workspace** (company). Ben (Acme) can never see Globex's data.
6. **Private notes** are encrypted in the browser with a team passphrase. The database only stores scrambled text.

**Result:** the automatic check scores **75/75** on every level we can run.

- then follow `SUBMISSION.md`

Yes, it's a **MERN project**: **MongoDB, Express, React, Node.js**. Nothing outside MERN, except two small extras that the assessment itself asked for.

## Languages and tools

| Part | What I used | Is it new for you? |
|---|---|---|
| Backend | **Node.js + Express** | Same as you know |
| Database | **MongoDB** | Same, but through the official `mongodb` driver instead of Mongoose (see below) |
| Frontend | **React** (with hooks: `useState`, `useEffect`) | Same |
| Language | **TypeScript** (`.ts` / `.tsx` files) | Small change, see below |
| Redis | Shared counters and login sessions | New, but used in only ~10 lines |
| `ws` | WebSocket library for live updates | Like Socket.io, but simpler |
| Vite | Runs and builds the React app | Like Create React App, just faster |

**About TypeScript:** it's **JavaScript with types**. The assessment's starter (`scaffold/`) already came in TypeScript, so I kept it. If you can read JS, you can read this: remove the type parts and it's plain JS.

```ts
// TypeScript
function claim(workspace: string, agent: string): Promise<boolean> { ... }

// Same thing in JavaScript
function claim(workspace, agent) { ... }
```

`interface Conversation { contact: string; ... }` just describes what an object looks like, like a Mongoose schema but only for the editor.

**Differences from a typical MERN tutorial:**
- **No Mongoose.** I used the official `mongodb` driver: `collection.insertOne()`, `findOneAndUpdate()`, `find().sort()`. These are the same method names Mongoose uses underneath.
- **No axios.** It uses the browser's built-in `fetch`.
- **No React Router.** There's only one page, which changes based on whether you're logged in.
- **No Socket.io.** It uses plain WebSocket.

## The files

### Backend: `scaffold/server/src/`
| File | What it does | Interview line |
|---|---|---|
| `index.ts` | **Start here.** The Express app: all routes (`app.get`, `app.post`), connects to Mongo and Redis, starts the server on `PORT`. | "This is my `server.js`." |
| `config.ts` | Reads `.env` values (ports, secrets, URLs). | Given by the assessment. |
| `db.ts` / `redis.ts` | Connect to MongoDB and Redis. | Given by the assessment. |
| `store.ts` | The "models": what each MongoDB collection looks like (`inbound`, `outbound`, `conversations`, `frames`, `notes`), plus indexes. | "Like my Mongoose models." |
| `webhook.ts` | Receives customer messages from Pigeon. Checks the signature, saves to Mongo, then replies 200. | "Save first, then say OK, so nothing is lost." |
| `outbox.ts` | Sends replies. Saves the reply as `queued`, and a background loop sends it to Pigeon, retries on failure and respects the rate limit. | "Like a job queue in MongoDB." |
| `inbox.ts` | Business logic: claim, release, close, list conversations, messages, notes. | "My controllers." |
| `auth.ts` | Login with the identity provider, sessions, and middleware `requireSession` / `requireMember`. | "Like JWT auth middleware, but the session is stored in Redis." |
| `realtime.ts` | WebSocket: pushes live updates to the browser. | "Like Socket.io's `emit`." |
| `core.test.ts` | 3 tests (signature, claim race, status order). | Run with `npm test`. |

### Frontend: `scaffold/web/src/`
| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `main.tsx` | Renders `<App />` (same as CRA's `index.js`). |
| `App.tsx` | Checks whether you're logged in (`/api/me`), then shows the login page or the inbox, plus the top bar. |
| `api.ts` | A small `fetch` helper and the data types. |
| `useLiveUpdates.ts` | Custom hook that opens the WebSocket and reconnects if it drops. |
| `notesCrypto.ts` | Encrypts and decrypts private notes (browser's built-in crypto). |
| `avatar.ts` | Picks a colour for each customer avatar. |
| `styles.css` | All styling, plain CSS (no Tailwind or Bootstrap). |
| `components/LoginPage.tsx` | Login screen. |
| `components/Inbox.tsx` | Left list, tabs, overview counters. |
| `components/ConversationView.tsx` | Chat messages, reply box, Claim / Release / Close buttons. |
| `components/NotesPanel.tsx` | Private notes panel. |

### Root files
- `README.md`: how to run it
- `DECISIONS.md`: what was built and cut, and known problems
- `PROTOCOL.md`: how note encryption works
- `switchboard.json`: tells the grader how to start the server

The folders `harness/`, `pigeon/`, `idp/` and `paybox/` were **given by the assessment**. We didn't write them, so you don't need to explain them.

## Suggested reading order in VS Code (about 15 minutes)
1. `server/src/index.ts`: see all the routes.
2. `server/src/inbox.ts`, the `claim` function: understand Claim.
3. `server/src/webhook.ts`: how a message comes in.
4. `web/src/App.tsx`, then `components/ConversationView.tsx`: how the UI calls the API.

Ask me about any file or line and I'll explain it in simple words.

Time is 6:53 PM. Before 7:50 we still need one final `npm run check:full` and the `ai-logs/` export.
